title: Whirlwind marginal checking reborn: live voltage-margin sweeps retire weak rows
idea: MIT Whirlwind and SAGE found dying tubes before they failed by deliberately lowering supply voltages during maintenance ('marginal checking'). The controller does this online: one subarray at a time is copied aside and exercised at VARY -60 mV, 4x stretched refresh and a skewed sense reference; any cell that fails under margin is logged and remapped before it can fail at nominal settings.
why: Retention tail and VRT (fact 3): catching marginal cells early lets the nominal refresh interval stretch 2-4x (refresh energy -50-75%) and lets vendors screen less aggressively at test; ~5-10% cost per bit from yield.

title: Williams-tube interlaced raster: rotating row interlace starves row hammer
idea: Williams-tube memories limited the 'read-around ratio' (charge spill from reading neighbouring spots) by interlacing the raster so neighbours were regenerated before spill accumulated. Logical rows map to physical rows through an interlace whose stride and phase rotate every 1/16 of the refresh window, and the migration piggybacks on refresh (each refresh reads a row and writes it into its new slot), so no aggressor keeps the same physical victims long enough to reach ~1k activations.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): disturb per victim is capped per phase instead of per window, ~16x margin with no per-row counters; periphery cost is one address-permutation unit per bank.

title: Bubble-memory bootloop: self-stored subarray defect map replaces fuse banks
idea: Magnetic bubble chips shipped with up to ~10% dead minor loops, listed in an on-chip 'bootloop' read at power-up. Design DRAM dies with ~12% spare subarrays and store the bad-subarray map in a few DRAM rows spread over several banks with 15x repetition coding, loaded into the address translator at boot and appended in the field as new failures appear.
why: Yield, periphery and capital (facts 4, 7): removes laser-fuse banks and lets aggressive cells or 3D tiers ship with clustered defects; ~15-25% more sellable dies per wafer at risky nodes.

title: Bell Model V two-out-of-five revival: reference-free top-k sensing
idea: Bell Labs relay computers stored digits in 2-out-of-5 constant-weight codes so every word checked itself. Store each 64-bit word as a 68-cell constant-weight codeword with exactly 34 charged cells (C(68,34) is about 2^64.6); instead of comparing each cell to a fixed Vref, a winner-take-all network marks the 34 highest-voltage cells as charged, so uniform decay, temperature drift and plate noise cancel out.
why: Retention tail and voltage floor (facts 3, 10): data survive until cells swap rank, not until they cross Vref, allowing ~4-8x longer refresh or ~40% less Cs, for 6% cell overhead plus detection of any weight-changing error.

title: Masoretic letter counts as Berger tags catch every one-way decay
idea: Masoretic scribes verified scrolls by counting letters, which exposes any omission. DRAM retention loss is one-way (charged to discharged, per physical cell polarity), so each 64-bit word carries a 7-bit complemented count of physically charged cells (a Berger code): any number of leakage flips lowers the data count and raises the tag, so detection is guaranteed, and on mismatch the controller re-reads with a lowered reference to locate the faded cells.
why: Retention tail (fact 3): guaranteed detection of all leakage errors for 7 bits per 64 lets refresh be relaxed 2-4x safely with a repair fallback, roughly halving refresh's 16-33% share of idle power.

title: Selectron holding-beam revival: global flood pulse re-latches every cell
idea: RCA's Selectron kept every bit stable with a flood of 'holding' electrons that pushed each eyelet to the nearer of two stable potentials. Give each storage node a weak bistable element (an ovonic threshold switch to a shared flood line plus a high-resistance leak) so one flood pulse every ~64 ms tops up every node still above threshold while discharged nodes stay low, restoring the whole array at once with no row activation and no bitline swing.
why: Refresh energy and bandwidth (facts 3, 9): replaces ~46 fJ/bit row-by-row refresh with one array-wide pulse (goal ~5x less energy), returns 10-20% of bandwidth and removes refresh activations that add to hammer stress.

title: Intel 1103 gain cells hold parity: physics diversity decorrelates failures
idea: Intel's 1970 1103 used a 3T cell read non-destructively through a gain transistor. Keep data in 1T1C cells but store the ECC check bits in a separate stripe of 3T gain cells, which have no capacitor, leak by a different mechanism and are not disturbed by wordline hammering, so one row event or leaky subarray cannot corrupt data and parity together.
why: Row hammer and retention tails (facts 3, 9): common-cause failures defeat ECC; diverse parity storage raises the effective correction of the same code, letting the data array run ~2x longer refresh with SECDED-sized overhead.

title: Von Neumann multiplexed bundles make defect-ridden 3D DRAM tiers usable
idea: Von Neumann's 1956 'probabilistic logics' built reliable organs from bundles of unreliable lines followed by a restoring majority stage. In stacked 3D DRAM, regions mapped as weak write each bit into vertically aligned cells on three different tiers and read them through a 3-input restoring sense stage, so one defective tier per column is harmless; a per-tier quality map keeps healthy regions in one-bit-per-cell mode.
why: No manufacturable 3D cell (fact 2): tier yield compounds over 26+ tiers; bundling tolerates per-tier defect rates near 1e-3 instead of 1e-7, so cheap tiers with weak lateral transistors become usable, paying 3x cells only where needed.

title: Moore-Shannon quadded relays revived as stacked series access transistors
idea: Moore and Shannon (1956) built reliable switching networks from crummy relays by series-parallel quadding. Build each vertical-channel access device as two gate segments stacked along the same pillar and driven by one wordline; a cell leaks only if both segments carry tail defects (trap-assisted GIDL, junction traps), which squares the tail probability, and in 4F2 vertical cells the second gate costs height, not area.
why: Access-leakage tail (fact 3): tail fraction ~1e-5 to ~1e-10, so refresh is set by the bulk distribution (~1 s instead of 64 ms), saving most of the 16-33% idle refresh power; on-current falls ~2x, recovered with pillar height.

title: Reed's 1954 majority-logic decoder built into the sense-amp stripe
idea: Irving Reed decoded Reed-Muller codes with one layer of parity checks feeding majority gates, with no iterative algebra. Weak subarrays use a one-step majority-logic-decodable (273,191) difference-set code whose XOR checks and majority votes form a single gate layer beside the column multiplexer, correcting 8 random errors per access in ~1 ns with no syndrome tables.
why: Weaker cells acceptable (facts 1, 3): tolerates raw BER ~1e-4 instead of ~1e-9 without a latency penalty, so Cs can drop ~30% or refresh stretch ~8x in those subarrays; ~40% parity there, applied only where cells are weak.

title: Mitsubishi cached DRAM revival: SRAM row cache absorbs hammering
idea: Mitsubishi's 1990s Cached DRAM and Ramtron's Enhanced DRAM put a small SRAM row cache on the die. Revive it as a hammer absorber: a 16-entry SRAM row cache per bank inserts a row on its second activation within a window, so repeat activations of hot rows are served from SRAM while the physical wordline stays closed, with an eviction counter that triggers neighbour restore if an attacker thrashes the cache.
why: Row hammer and activation energy (facts 8, 9): bounds physical ACTs per row below the ~1k flip threshold without per-row counters and cuts activation energy for hot rows ~90%; die area +2-3%.

title: Apollo restart protection: phase-table rollback survives uncorrectable DRAM errors
idea: The Apollo Guidance Computer survived its 1202 alarms because software recorded restart-phase waypoints and resumed from the last one after a hardware restart. Runtimes keep per-task phase points with a small undo log of dirty lines in a strongly protected region; when the controller reports an uncorrectable error, only the affected task rolls back to its last phase and recomputes.
why: Error tolerance for cheaper memory: turns DUEs from node outages into millisecond recomputes, so fleets can accept 10-100x higher raw DUE rates from relaxed refresh, lighter ECC or lower-binned dies; ~10-20% lower cost per usable bit.

title: Poppelbaum stochastic counts store KV-cache LSBs in unrefreshed rows
idea: 1960s stochastic computers (Gaines, Poppelbaum) coded numbers as a count of 1s, so one flipped bit moves the value by one quantum instead of wrecking it. Each 8-bit KV-cache value keeps its 5 MSBs in normally refreshed rows and its 3 LSBs as a 7-cell count code in rows refreshed 10x less often; a decay flip there shifts the value by exactly 1 LSB, which attention tolerates.
why: Refresh energy and bandwidth (fact 3): over half the cells of the fastest-growing AI tier skip ~90% of refresh at a bounded accuracy cost; density cost ~1.5x on those values, so it pays only for hot, short-lived tensors.

title: Toshiba's forgotten 4-level DRAM, Gray-mapped like Frank Gray's tube
idea: Toshiba (1989) and NEC (1996) demonstrated 2-bit/cell DRAM and then dropped it; Frank Gray's 1947 PCM coding tube used reflected-binary code so a beam landing between zones made only a one-bit error. Store 2 bits per cell as four charge levels with Gray mapping, read by a two-step charge-sharing sense amp, so leakage drift into the adjacent level costs one bit, which a light per-word BCH repairs.
why: Density and cost per bit (fact 4): ~1.8x bits per area without a litho node; Gray mapping converts the dominant MLC failure (one-level drift) into single-bit errors; needs ~2x refresh and much tighter sensing.

title: Core-memory inhibit winding revived as anti-hammer neighbour counter-pulse
idea: Coincident-current core planes drove an 'inhibit' current through cores that must not switch, cancelling the half-select field. Each time a wordline rises, the drivers of its two physical neighbours apply a brief matched negative counter-pulse (~-0.3 V for the rise time) that cancels the capacitive kick and suppresses electron injection from the aggressor channel into neighbouring storage nodes, the mechanisms behind hammer flips.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): aims to push the flip threshold from ~1k to 10k+ activations, cutting mitigation refresh and counter overhead; costs ~5% extra wordline-driver energy.

title: Plated-wire NDRO strip stores row-hammer counters without disturbing DRAM
idea: Plated-wire memory (UNIVAC 1110, Voyager) read non-destructively by tilting magnetization slightly and sensing its elastic return. Move DDR5 PRAC-style per-row activation counters out of the DRAM rows into a small magnetic or ferroelectric NDRO counter strip on the bank periphery, read without restore and updated in the background, so counting adds no read-modify-write timing and cannot itself be hammered.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): in-array PRAC counters cost ~10% of tRC and bandwidth; an NDRO strip keeps exact per-row counts without that penalty for ~1-2% area.

title: No. 1 ESS audit programs scan for silent DRAM corruption
idea: Bell's No. 1 ESS ran continuous audit programs that walked switching tables, checked structural invariants and repaired corrupted records. Runtimes run a low-priority auditor that checks invariants of live data (pointer ranges, allocator headers, type tags, per-block hashes of model weights) at ~1% CPU and repairs from replicas or recomputes, catching silent corruption that slips past ECC.
why: Bounding silent data corruption lets operators relax refresh and ECC strength on bulk memory (refresh energy -30-50%) while keeping corruption risk at today's level.

title: Tape AC-bias revival: dithered refresh pulses park VRT traps
idea: Magnetic tape needed a high-frequency AC bias to shake domains out of hysteresis and record linearly. Variable-retention-time cells toggle because one defect near the storage junction flips between configurations; a short high-frequency dither on the cell plate or wordline-low level during refresh, tuned to drive metastable traps into their low-leakage configuration, keeps VRT cells in the long-retention state most of the time.
why: Retention tail and VRT (fact 3): VRT defeats retention profiling and forces worst-case refresh; parking traps would let profiled multi-rate refresh work, giving ~2-4x longer average refresh intervals.

title: Babbage's locking detents: time-to-latch flags ambiguous bits as erasures
idea: Babbage designed the Difference Engine to jam rather than pass a figure wheel resting between two digits. Each sense-amp group gets a tiny timer measuring latch resolution time (which grows as ln(1/dV)); slow-resolving bits are flagged as erasures and the ECC decodes with their positions known, which doubles what the same parity repairs (a SECDED code corrects 2-3 erasures).
why: Retention tail and sense margin (facts 1, 3): faded cells become located erasures instead of silent flips, so refresh can stretch ~2-4x or Cs shrink ~25% with unchanged ECC overhead; a few transistors per sense-amp group.

title: Drum clock-track revival: leaky canary columns time each subarray's refresh
idea: Magnetic drums carried a dedicated clock track that timed everything else on the drum. Each subarray gets one canary column of cells built deliberately at the leaky tail (shorter gate, extra junction implant) that is rewritten at every refresh; the subarray is refreshed only when canaries start failing sensing, so the interval tracks local temperature, voltage and aging instead of a fixed 64 ms.
why: Refresh energy (fact 3): most subarrays most of the time could run 3-8x longer intervals; area ~0.2%.

title: Holographic page spreading: Hadamard-encode weights so failures become noise
idea: 1970s holographic memories spread every bit across the whole plate, so a scratch only added noise. Before writing neural-network weight pages, a fast Walsh-Hadamard transform is applied across each 2 KB block; dead bitlines, hammered regions or retention clusters then come back after the inverse transform as low-amplitude noise spread over all weights, which models tolerate without ECC.
why: Error tolerance for the largest AI capacity tier: removes 12.5% ECC overhead and repair for weight memory and tolerates clustered faults, for ~log2(N) adds per value in the base die.

title: Geiger ratemeter diode pump: one extra cell integrates row activations
idea: 1950s Geiger-counter ratemeters used a diode pump that added a fixed charge packet per pulse to a leaky capacitor, giving a time-windowed count with no logic. Each row gets one extra 'hammer cell' that receives a fixed charge quantum through a diode-connected device whenever its wordline fires, while natural leakage drains it; at refresh, a threshold sense reveals rows activated more than ~500 times recently and triggers neighbour restores.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): windowed activation counting for one cell per row (~0.01% area) instead of SRAM or in-array counters, with no timing penalty.

title: Goto's parametron revived: parametric bitline pumping senses tiny charges
idea: Eiichi Goto's 1954 parametron stored a bit as the phase of a parametrically pumped oscillation. Pump the bitline pair's MOS varactor at twice the sense frequency during sensing, so the cell's small charge seeds the phase of an oscillation that grows exponentially, with gain set by matched capacitors instead of threshold-mismatched latch transistors.
why: Capacitor charge wall and voltage floor (facts 1, 10): latch offset (~10-20 mV) dominates margin; parametric sensing could tolerate ~2x smaller signal, allowing Cs near 2.5 fF or longer retention.

title: Cray-2 Fluorinert revival: boiling-pinned memory retunes refresh without water
idea: The Cray-2 (1985) ran its stacked boards submerged in circulating Fluorinert. Immerse DIMMs and HBM in a low-GWP two-phase fluid boiling at ~50 C, which pins every die at that temperature, then calibrate refresh interval, sense trims and ECC strength once for 50 C instead of the 85-95 C worst case; vapour is condensed by dry coolers.
why: Water and refresh (fact 3): dry condensers need no evaporative towers (WUE ~1.8 to <0.1 L/kWh, >10x), and a pinned 50 C die leaks ~8x less than at 85 C, so refresh falls ~4-8x and the retention tail stops limiting weaker cells.

title: Pioneer-probe convolutional coding lets HBM run hot on dry coolers
idea: Pioneer 9 (1968) used convolutional codes with sequential decoding to pull data out of very noisy channels. HBM pages are encoded along each burst with a rate-15/16 tail-biting convolutional code decoded by a pipelined Viterbi in the logic base die, tolerating raw BER ~1e-3 at 6% overhead, enough to run the stack at ~115 C at the standard refresh rate.
why: Water: HBM's 85-95 C limit is usually the binding thermal constraint on accelerators; raising it ~20 C lets facilities use dry coolers year-round instead of evaporative towers (>10x less water) and also absorbs the retention tail (fact 3).

title: Delay-line mode: streamed weight reads double as refresh at 115 C
idea: In mercury delay lines, data were refreshed simply by circulating. LLM inference streams every weight row once per token batch (~10-30 ms), so the controller orders weight reads to touch every row within its hot retention window and marks those banks refresh-exempt, with a watchdog that issues real refresh whenever traffic pauses.
why: Water and refresh (fact 3): weight banks stay correct at 105-115 C, where refresh would otherwise quadruple, so memory no longer forces chilled or evaporative cooling (>10x less water with dry coolers); weight-memory refresh energy drops to ~0.

title: IBM 650 SOAP-style placement puts tolerant tensors in the hottest dies
idea: The IBM 650's SOAP assembler placed each instruction where the rotating drum would deliver it soonest. A placement compiler does the same with heat: from a thermal map of the HBM stack (top and centre dies run hottest) it places error-tolerant data (KV cache, activations, gradients) in the hottest banks with relaxed refresh and critical data (optimizer state, page tables) in the coolest, most protected banks.
why: Water: the stack's allowed average temperature rises ~10-15 C because only tolerant data sit in hot spots, enabling warm-water dry cooling without evaporation (>10x less facility water); refresh energy -30%.

title: Floppy soft-sectoring revival: per-region code strength formats dry-cleaned dies
idea: Soft-sectored floppies were formatted after manufacture around their actual media defects. After wafer test, firmware formats each subarray with an ECC strength chosen from its measured defect density (none, SECDED, BCH-4 or retire) and records it in a die format table, so the clustered, edge-heavy particle defects of an all-dry clean flow (cryogenic aerosol, radical plasma, vapour HF) cost a few percent of capacity instead of whole dies.
why: Water: wet cleans and rinses are ~70-80% of a DRAM fab's ultrapure water; an all-dry flow plus air-cooled chillers is a ~10x water cut, and soft formatting absorbs its ~3-5x higher particle defectivity at roughly flat cost per bit.

title: Voyager concatenated coding across HBM dies forgives dry-bonded voids
idea: Voyager paired a convolutional inner code with a Reed-Solomon outer code so bursts the inner code missed were cleaned up. In HBM, each die keeps a light inner code while an outer Reed-Solomon code spans corresponding banks of all 12-16 dies (one symbol per die), so a die region lost to a bonding void or open TSV is just an erasure the outer code fills.
why: Water and HBM yield (fact 6): lets stacks use dry plasma-activated bonding and skip the CMP and post-CMP wet cleans that hybrid bonding needs (~10x less water in stacking) while recovering the 20-30% stack-yield loss; 6-12% outer-code overhead.

title: Dolby pre-emphasis writes overdrive leaky rows from recycled-water fabs
idea: Dolby noise reduction boosted quiet signals when recording and cut them on playback. Rows profiled as leaky are written with ~+150 mV boosted array voltage and a longer write time (pre-emphasis) and read with a matching reference shift (de-emphasis) from a row-class table, so cells with extra junction leakage still hold enough charge across a normal refresh interval.
why: Water: lets the fab run a ~90-95% closed rinse loop at 1-5 MOhm-cm instead of once-through 18 MOhm-cm ultrapure water (~10x less fresh water), whose trace metals widen the leakage tail (fact 3); pre-emphasis recovers ~2x retention on affected rows.

title: Three-head tape deck read-after-write verifies dry-cleaned contact writes
idea: Three-head tape decks read each bit back milliseconds after recording to confirm it. Write drivers add a fast verify: right after a write to a row flagged high-resistance, the sense amp re-senses the restored cells before precharge and extends tWR or rewrites only if the level is short, covering contacts that are 2-3x more resistive.
why: Water: lets the fab drop wet HF/SC1 pre-metal and contact cleans for dry remote-plasma cleans, which leave higher contact resistance and slow writes (the tWR failure mode); with dry cleans elsewhere this enables the ~10x ultrapure-water cut, adding tWR only on flagged rows.

title: Twistor revival: thermally drawn memory fibre, reel-tested, bad segments skipped
idea: Bell's twistor memory stored bits along woven magnetic wires. Thermally draw a multi-material preform (glass or polymer cladding, embedded metal wordlines, a ferroelectric or charge-storing core) into kilometres of memory fibre in a fully dry process; a reel-to-reel tester maps bad segments the way tape drives map defects, and good segments are woven into mats addressed like twistor planes.
why: Water and capital (fact 4): fibre drawing needs no ultrapure-water wet cleans (>10x less water than a wafer flow) and little capital, and segment mapping makes a crude process usable; density and speed are far from DRAM-class today.

title: CRT rejuvenator revival: on-die microheaters anneal away retention traps
idea: 1950s TV-tube rejuvenators briefly overdrove the cathode heater to restore emission. Polysilicon microheaters under each bank let the controller move a bank's data out and pulse it to ~350 C for milliseconds against hydrogen-bearing passivation, re-passivating interface traps and dissolving the metal-related defects that create leaky tail cells, at power-up or in scheduled maintenance.
why: Water: contamination-induced leaky cells from lower-purity recycled rinse water and fewer clean steps are cured in the package, a path to ~10x less fresh water; also heals aging-related retention loss (fact 3); heater area ~1%.

title: Core-stack parity plane revived: XOR row rebuilds any killed wordline
idea: Many core memories carried an extra parity plane computed across all bit planes. Each subarray gets one XOR parity row, kept up to date in a small per-subarray SRAM latch on every write and written back at refresh, so a whole wordline lost to a particle short, a hammer burst or a stuck driver is rebuilt from the other rows and remapped in the field.
why: Water: whole-wordline kills are the dominant yield loss from particles left by dry cleaning; rebuilding them lets an all-dry, ~10x-lower-water flow hold yield for ~0.2% extra rows plus latch area.

title: Core-sorting bins: grade dry-process DRAM into tiers, sell every die
idea: Core-memory makers tested every ferrite core and sorted them into hysteresis grades for different products. A DRAM maker running an all-dry, water-lean fab tests each die for retention and defect class and sells three grades with their own pricing and warranties: server ECC, AI-tensor (relaxed retention handled by the controller) and edge (reduced capacity, soft-formatted).
why: Water and cost per bit: the dry flow's wider defect spread becomes a product mix instead of a yield loss, which pays for converting a fab to ~10x less ultrapure water; ~95% of dies sold instead of ~85%.

title: MIL-STD-883 screening classes revived as a water-lean JEDEC W-grade
idea: MIL-STD-883 defined screening classes so buyers could trade reliability testing against cost. A JEDEC and CHIPS-backed 'W-grade' DRAM class would specify relaxed raw retention (e.g., 16 ms at 85 C), mandatory on-die SEC with host-visible error telemetry, and a certified water cap of 10% of today's litres per GB, with federal buyers and hyperscalers committing volume to it.
why: Water and U.S. manufacturability: a standard makes dry-clean, recycled-water U.S. fabs sellable at scale (~10x less water per GB) despite weaker cells by moving the reliability burden to the system, where it is cheaper.

title: Analog-computer droop compensation: time-aware sense references for hot memory
idea: Analog computers corrected sample-and-hold capacitors for their known droop by predicting the decay. The controller knows each row's age since restore from the refresh pointer (with a coarse per-subarray flag for recent writes) and reads the die temperature, then lowers the sense reference along the expected decay curve, so a cell that has lost 40% of its charge still reads correctly.
why: Water and retention (fact 3): memory runs at 105-110 C with standard refresh instead of 4x refresh, so facilities can use dry coolers instead of evaporative towers (>10x less water); ~2x retention margin at near-zero area.

title: Core-stack thermistor compensation revived: temperature-tracking negative wordline bias
idea: Core memories put thermistors in the stack to retune drive currents as ferrite properties drifted with temperature. Each subarray sets its negative wordline-low voltage and body bias from a local temperature sensor and replica leakage cells that find, in real time, the minimum of subthreshold leakage plus GIDL (which moves with temperature), instead of using one worst-case bias.
why: Water and leakage tail (fact 3): holding the hot leakage tail ~3x lower lets DRAM run 10-15 C hotter at the same refresh rate, removing the need for chilled or evaporative cooling (>10x less water with dry coolers).

title: Core-stack strobe tuning revived: per-mat sense trims absorb CMP-free topography
idea: Core-memory stacks were tuned individually at the factory, with sense-strobe delay and threshold set per stack. At wafer test each DRAM mat is characterized and given its own sense-reference offset, sense-enable delay and wordline boost in a trim table, so a wafer planarized by dry etch-back and spin-on glass instead of CMP (leaving 15-20 nm topography and wider cell variation) still reads with full margin.
why: Water: CMP and post-CMP cleans are a large share of fab ultrapure water; dropping them along with wet cleans is the route to ~10x less water, and trims recover ~30-50 mV of lost margin for ~1 kb of trim storage per die.

title: Vacuum-tube getter flash revived: sacrificial getter soaks recycled-water metals
idea: Vacuum tubes carried a barium getter, flashed after sealing, that soaked up residual gas for the tube's whole life. A sacrificial gettering layer (carbon/phosphorus co-implant or a polysilicon sink) under each array, plus a final low-temperature 'getter flash' anneal, pulls Fe, Cu and Ni away from storage junctions, so trace metals from lower-purity recycled rinse water never reach the cells.
why: Water: makes a ~90-95% closed rinse loop at 1-5 MOhm-cm acceptable (~10x less fresh water) by shielding the retention tail (fact 3) from the metals that loop carries.

title: VCR dropout compensator revival: conceal faulty words in AI tensors
idea: VCRs hid tape dropouts by substituting the previous scan line from a delay line. The accelerator's memory controller keeps a map of known-bad or uncorrectable words in tensor memory and on access substitutes a predicted value (neighbouring element, channel mean, or zero for activations) instead of trapping or retrying, logging each event.
why: Water: lets AI-tensor DRAM from an all-dry, ~10x-lower-water fab ship without repair fuses or spare rows, because scattered point defects are concealed instead of repaired; ~10% less capacity and ECC overhead.

title: Relay computer revival: NEMS contact access switches with zero off-leakage
idea: Bell Labs and Harvard relay computers switched bits with metal contacts that had no leakage when open. Replace the access transistor with a vertical nano-electromechanical contact switch (a ~10 nm air-gap cantilever pulled in by the wordline) released with dry vapour HF, so an open cell has essentially no leakage path and retention is set by dielectric leakage (minutes) even at 125 C.
why: Water and refresh (facts 3, 10): removing the access-leakage tail lets memory run at 125 C with near-zero refresh, so datacentres can use dry coolers (>10x less water), and dry release avoids wet MEMS steps; contact wear (~1e15 cycles needed) is the main risk.

title: Metallized-film self-healing: clearing pulses isolate pinholes in dry-processed capacitors
idea: Bosch's 1930s metallized-paper capacitors healed themselves when a breakdown arc vaporized the thin electrode around the flaw. The DRAM capacitor's top electrode becomes an ultrathin segmented TiN film, and at wafer sort a controlled overvoltage clearing pulse drives current through any pinhole hard enough to oxidize the electrode locally, turning a shorted or leaky capacitor into a slightly smaller good one.
why: Water: capacitor modules cleaned dry (no wet cleans after high-aspect-ratio etch or between high-k layers) carry more particles and pinholes; self-clearing restores yield and the retention tail, enabling the all-dry ~10x water cut at a Cs loss of ~2-5% on healed cells.

title: Early FeRAM imprint fix revived: periodic polarity flips cancel sense-amp aging
idea: Early FeRAMs fought imprint, where a cell held in one state too long comes to prefer it, and periodic inverted rewriting was a classic remedy. DRAM sense-amp latches age asymmetrically (BTI drift) when data sit unchanged for months at high temperature, so every N refresh epochs each row is rewritten inverted under a per-row polarity bit and both latch halves age equally.
why: Water: sense-amp offset drift is a key barrier to 105-115 C operation over 5+ years; cancelling it lets memory run hot enough for dry coolers (>10x less water) while keeping sense margin for weak cells (fact 1).

title: Floppy FM/MFM density switching: twin-cell mode during heat waves
idea: Floppy drives read and wrote either single density (FM) or double density (MFM) on the same media. Subarrays carry a mode bit: in normal weather they run one bit per cell, and on the hottest days the OS migrates cold data out and flips selected subarrays into twin-cell complementary mode, doubling signal and roughly tripling retention so error rates hold at higher coolant temperature.
why: Water: most of a facility's annual evaporative water goes to its hottest few hundred hours; trading ~25% capacity during those hours lets dry coolers carry the whole year (>10x less water).

title: 1970s ceramic hermetic packaging revived: corrosion-proof memory for free-air cooling
idea: Military DRAMs of the 1970s sat in hermetic ceramic (CERDIP) packages that kept moisture and sulfur out. DIMMs and HBM packages get ALD alumina/parylene stacks or glass-frit hermetic lids plus silver-free, sulfur-resistant contacts, so memory survives unconditioned outside air (high humidity, sulfur creep corrosion) and facilities can cool with direct outside air without humidification.
why: Water: direct free-air cooling without evaporative humidity control uses ~0 L/kWh (>10x vs evaporative), and corrosion plus humidity-driven leakage are the memory failure modes that block it today.
